templates.name: Main idea, informational study report (incl. explainer and scholar-argument passages)

items.passage: Dhajji dewari, a building method of the western Himalayas, divides each wall’s timber frame into small panels filled with stone or brick set in mud mortar. After a 2005 earthquake in Kashmir, more than 100,000 homes were rebuilt with the method, though its structural behavior had received little study. Modeling a typical house, engineers at the firm Arup and conservationist Randolph Langenbach determined that the walls dissipate seismic energy partly through friction as the masonry panels shift against the frame. This absorption of energy, they found, increases when more weight presses on the panels.
items.stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about dhajji dewari buildings that are more than one story tall?
options: Their ground-floor walls would likely need more timber bracing than those of one-story houses, since those walls must carry the weight of the floors above.
The weight of their upper floors could hold the masonry panels of the ground-floor walls in place, making those walls less able to absorb an earthquake’s energy.
Their ground-floor walls, pressed down by the floors above, could absorb more of an earthquake’s energy than the walls of a one-story house.
They were likely rebuilt less often than one-story houses after the 2005 earthquake, since the method’s structural behavior had received little study.
items.explanation: The text says that the walls absorb seismic energy partly through friction as the panels shift against the frame and that this absorption increases when more weight presses on the panels. In a building of more than one story, the floors above press down on the ground-floor walls, so those walls carry more weight than the walls of a one-story house and could therefore absorb more energy.

A.why_wrong: The ground-floor walls do carry the floors above, but the text never mentions bracing; the only effect of extra weight it reports is that the walls absorb more energy.

B.why_wrong: The engineers found that energy absorption increases when more weight presses on the panels, so the weight of upper floors would help the ground-floor walls rather than weaken them.

D.why_wrong: The text does say the method had received little study, but it gives no figures for houses of different heights and never links the lack of study to which houses were rebuilt.

sources.what: Hicyilmaz, Wilcock, Izatt, da Silva and Langenbach, Seismic Performance of Dhajji Dewari, 15th WCEE 2012: over 100,000 homes rebuilt with dhajji dewari after the 2005 Kashmir earthquake; limited research; energy dissipated through friction between masonry panels and timber frame; increased overburden increases energy absorption, evidence that two or more storeys may be satisfactory

items.notes: Technology and engineering. Premise 1: friction between panels and frame absorbs energy; premise 2: more weight on the panels means more absorption; unstated conclusion: upper floors load the lower walls and may help them. The paper states that conclusion itself ("two or even more storey structures may be satisfactory"); the key keeps its hedge (could).

fixes: hardened to a fair band 6: key paraphrased into a comparison with one-story walls (two steps: floors above load the ground-floor walls; more load means more absorption); A and D now pair a true premise (walls carry the floors above; little study) with an unsupported conclusion; B is the intuitive reversal (weight pins the panels) in place of the stronger-mortar option

band7.why: Planned band 6 (wave-2 plan sets every Central Ideas hard cell to 6). After hardening: two-step key with a comparison, all three distractors partly right, recipes UNS, CON, UNS; no stance word or aside, so not band 7.

items.passage: In 1994, San Francisco voters extended rent control, which limits how much landlords may raise the rent of a sitting tenant, to small apartment buildings constructed before 1980. Studying the following decades, economists Rebecca Diamond, Timothy McQuade, and Franklin Qian found that the change helped covered tenants remain in their homes. But landlords of the newly covered buildings cut the number of units they offered for rent by 15 percent, often by selling units to owner-occupants or by redeveloping their buildings, shrinking the city’s supply of rental housing.
items.stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about the 1994 expansion of rent control in San Francisco?
options: It likely made renting more costly for many tenants who were not covered by it, even as it helped those who were.
It helped covered tenants remain in their homes but likely had little effect on the number of apartments available to other renters in the city.
It likely benefited tenants in the newly covered buildings more than tenants in buildings that had been covered by rent control before 1994.
It likely reduced the demand for rental housing in San Francisco by making landlords less willing to offer apartments to tenants.
items.explanation: The text says that the expansion helped covered tenants stay in their homes but that landlords of the covered buildings cut the units they offered for rent by 15 percent, shrinking the city’s supply of rental housing. With fewer apartments available to the same pool of renters, those who were not protected by the law would likely have faced higher rents, so the law most likely helped one group of tenants while raising costs for others.

B.why_wrong: The first half is true, but the landlords’ 15 percent cut shrank the city’s supply of rental housing, so the expansion did affect the apartments available to other renters.

C.why_wrong: The text never mentions buildings covered by rent control before 1994, so it gives no basis for comparing how much the two groups of tenants benefited.

D.why_wrong: Landlords did become less willing to offer apartments, but that reduced the supply of rental units, not renters’ demand for them; the text says nothing about demand falling.

sources.what: Diamond, McQuade and Qian, NBER w24181 / AER 2019: rent control increased renters’ probability of staying at their addresses; treated landlords reduced rental housing supply by 15 percent (selling to owner-occupants, redeveloping), causing a 5.1 percent city-wide rent increase; paper body: the 1994 ballot initiative created rent control protections for small multifamily housing built prior to 1980

items.notes: Social science (urban economics). Premises: covered tenants helped; landlords cut rental units by 15 percent, reducing the city's rental supply. Unstated conclusion (stated in the paper): the lost supply raised market rents for others. Paper's 5.1 percent city-wide figure left out so the key stays an inference; the supply clause (paper: reduced rental housing supply) gives the inference a textual basis.

fixes: source body (NBER w24181 pdf) confirms the 1994 ballot initiative for small multifamily buildings built before 1980
added the clause that the cut shrank the city's supply of rental housing (paper: reduced rental housing supply) so the key no longer needs an outside supply step
hardened: B is now a half-true compound (helped covered tenants, but little effect on supply), C an invented comparison with pre-1994 covered buildings; key reworded

band7.why: Planned band 6. Key needs two links (cut shrinks supply; less supply raises rents for others), distractors CON-half, CMP, TWI (supply read as demand); options 21 to 25 words. No stance word or third statement, so strong band 6.

items.passage: Analyzing classical recordings made before the mid-1950s, musicologist Daniel Leech-Wilkinson documented two stylistic transformations that unfolded concurrently. Portamento, an audible slide from one note to the next, was a routine expressive device on early recordings but grew gradually less prevalent; by the late 1940s, performers no longer employed it as a matter of course. Meanwhile, vibrato, a slight oscillation in pitch that also lends a note expressive warmth, became progressively slower and wider, and its most pronounced widening occurred in the late 1940s and early 1950s.
items.stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about the changes that Leech-Wilkinson traced?
options: Because both techniques gave notes expressive warmth, performers likely used portamento more often as their vibrato grew slower and wider.
Portamento likely fell out of use because early recording equipment could not clearly capture slides from one note to the next.
The most pronounced widening of vibrato likely came in the early decades of recording, when portamento was still a routine part of performers’ playing.
Performers may have turned to vibrato for some of the expressive effect that portamento had once given their playing.
items.explanation: The text presents both techniques as expressive (vibrato “also” lends a note expressive warmth) and says that portamento grew less common over the same decades in which vibrato grew slower and wider, with vibrato’s sharpest widening coming just as portamento stopped being routine. This timing suggests that performers may have shifted some of the expressive work once done by portamento to vibrato.

A.why_wrong: Both techniques are described as expressive, but portamento grew less common while vibrato grew slower and wider, so performers used it less often, not more.

B.why_wrong: Portamento was routine on early recordings, so early equipment did capture it; the text gives no technical cause for its decline.

C.why_wrong: Portamento was routine on early recordings, but the text places vibrato’s most pronounced widening in the late 1940s and early 1950s, when performers no longer used portamento as a matter of course.

sources.what: Leech-Wilkinson, The Changing Sound of Music (CHARM), ch. 7: as portamento gradually declined, vibrato slowed and widened; some of the expressive work done by portamento was probably transferring to vibrato; the greatest increase in vibrato width came in the later 1940s and early 50s, when portamento ceased to be routine

Wayback Machine copy of the same CHARM chapter 7 (live page sits behind a bot check): portamento declined as vibrato slowed and widened; some expressive work probably transferred to vibrato; greatest widening in the later 1940s and early 50s

items.notes: Arts (music, performance history). The key carries the source's own hedge ("It seems reasonable to suggest"), as may have. The chapter frames the change as one of the first half of the twentieth century without limiting it to strings (the violin data are in chapter 5), so the passage says classical recordings. Options A and C each pair a true clause with a reversed relation (frequency, timing).

fixes: live CHARM URL is behind a bot wall; text confirmed on the Wayback copy (chapter 7: expressive work transferring from portamento to vibrato; greatest vibrato widening in the later 1940s and early 50s)
passage no longer limits the study to string performances (chapter 7 does not; violin data are in chapter 5): now classical recordings made before the mid-1950s, stem and options say performers
hardened: A (both expressive, so more portamento) and C (peak widening placed in the early decades, when portamento was routine) are partly right with one reversed relation; key paraphrased

band7.why: Planned band 6. Key joins three statements (both expressive, concurrent change, timing), distractors CON-half, UNS, CON-half; a band-7 shape in parts but the key is reachable from the word also, so band 6.

items.passage: Engineered superhydrophobic surfaces repel water so effectively that a thin film of air clings to them under water, but in flowing water they typically lose that film within hours. The floating fern Salvinia molesta, by contrast, can retain its air layer for weeks. Botanist Wilhelm Barthlott and colleagues identified the reason: although the minute whisk-shaped hairs on its leaves repel water, each hair’s tip is hydrophilic, or water-attracting, anchoring the surrounding water so that the trapped air cannot readily escape. Ship hulls designed on this principle could therefore encounter less friction.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Barthlott and colleagues found that the fern’s air layer outlasts those of engineered surfaces because the hairs on its leaves repel water more strongly than any material that engineers have yet produced.
Barthlott and colleagues traced the fern’s lasting air layer to hairs that repel water except at their tips, a design that could help ship hulls move through water more easily.
Barthlott and colleagues found that engineered surfaces lose their air layer within hours because, unlike the fern’s hairs, those surfaces have tips that attract water.
Barthlott and colleagues showed that a ship hull coated with whisk-shaped hairs held its air layer for weeks and met less friction than other hulls did.
items.explanation: The text contrasts engineered water-repelling surfaces, which lose their air layer within hours, with the fern, which keeps its air layer for weeks. It then gives Barthlott and colleagues’ explanation: the fern’s hairs repel water, but their water-attracting tips anchor the surrounding water so the air cannot escape. It ends by noting that hulls built on this principle could meet less friction. Choice B states both the finding and its possible use.

A.why_wrong: The fern’s air layer does outlast those of engineered surfaces, but the text credits the hairs’ water-attracting tips, not stronger water repellence, and it never ranks the fern against every engineered material.

C.why_wrong: Engineered surfaces do lose their air layer within hours, but it is the fern’s hairs that have water-attracting tips, which hold the air in place; the text says nothing about tips on engineered surfaces.

D.why_wrong: The text says only that hulls designed on this principle could encounter less friction; it does not say that such a hull was built or tested.

sources.what: University of Bonn release on Barthlott et al., Advanced Materials 2010 (The Salvinia Paradox): the fern keeps an air layer for weeks under water; artificial superhydrophobic layers disappear within hours in moving water; hairs are hydrophobic but their tips hydrophilic, stapling water so air cannot escape; possible hulls with reduced friction

items.notes: Technology and engineering (biomimetics). Spread main idea: finding in the middle, application at the end; the key joins them. The release's 10 percent fuel estimate is left out.

fixes: hardened: key paraphrased (hairs that repel water except at their tips; hulls move through water more easily); C now swaps which surface has water-attracting tips; D claims a tested hull

band7.why: Planned band 6. Main idea joins finding and application; distractors TWI (wrong mechanism), TWI (swapped entity), OVR; mean option length 28. Overstatement recipe and no stance word keep it band 6.

items.passage: In seventeenth-century England, Robert Boyle’s famous experiments with the air pump relied on paid assistants who built and operated the apparatus and carried out many of the trials. Boyle’s published reports, however, mention these workers only in passing and seldom name them. Historian of science Steven Shapin attributes this silence to the period’s conventions of credibility: an account of an experiment was trusted because it was told under a gentleman’s authority, and hired workers were not thought to possess such authority.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Shapin contends that Boyle’s reports pass over his assistants because, at the time, an account of an experiment was believed on the strength of its teller’s social rank.
Shapin argues that because hired workers were thought to lack a gentleman’s authority, Boyle’s experiments were doubted until he began carrying out the trials himself.
According to Shapin, Boyle depended on paid assistants more heavily than other gentlemen experimenters did, which is why his reports seldom name them.
According to Shapin, Boyle rarely named his assistants because their tasks were routine and contributed little to the outcome of his experiments.
items.explanation: The text first notes that Boyle’s assistants did much of the experimental work but are seldom mentioned in his reports, and then gives Shapin’s explanation: an account was trusted because it was told under a gentleman’s authority, and hired workers were not thought to have such authority. Choice A joins the observation and Shapin’s explanation, restating the gentleman’s authority as the teller’s social rank.

B.why_wrong: Hired workers were indeed thought to lack a gentleman’s authority, but the text never says Boyle’s experiments were doubted or that he took over the trials; his reports were trusted because he told them.

C.why_wrong: Boyle did rely on paid assistants, but the text never compares him with other gentlemen, and Shapin explains the silence by the period’s conventions of credibility.

D.why_wrong: The experiments relied on the assistants, who built and operated the apparatus and carried out many of the trials, and Shapin explains the silence by conventions of credibility.

sources.what: University of Houston, Engines of Our Ingenuity 350, on Shapin, The Invisible Technician (American Scientist 77:6, 1989): Boyle's experiments were commonly done by assistants; Boyle makes only fleeting reference to help in his lab (Papin the exception); what mattered was that the story was told under his authority

Science Musings (Chet Raymo, 1990) on Shapin, The Invisible Technician: the scientist and technician split grounded in social class; the servant's voice assumed to be included in the master's; scientists kept their gentlemanly status by insisting on the invisibility of assistants

items.notes: History of science (scholar's argument, like 3.20). Shapin's servant/gentleman framing kept general ("hired workers", "a gentleman's authority"), worded as the source states it; no claim that assistants made discoveries themselves.

fixes: added a second source for the gentleman versus servant framing (Shapin: servants' voice included in the master's; gentlemanly status kept by the invisibility of assistants)
hardened: key paraphrased (believed on the strength of its teller's social rank); B now starts from the true point that hired workers lacked authority, C from the true reliance on paid assistants

band7.why: Planned band 6. Key paraphrases authority as social rank; distractors TWI, CMP, CON, each partly right. Options 22 to 28 words; one-step explanation in the passage, so band 6.

items.passage: Accounts of the annexation of Hawaiʻi by the United States in 1898 long depicted Native Hawaiians as having accepted the loss of their nation with little resistance. While researching Hawaiian-language sources in the 1990s, however, political scientist Noenoe Silva located in the US National Archives an 1897 petition opposing annexation, organized by Native Hawaiian political associations and bearing more than 21,000 signatures. Presented to the US Senate, the petition contributed to the defeat of an annexation treaty, although the islands were annexed through other means the following year.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Although Native Hawaiians were long described as accepting annexation, a petition that Silva located shows that their opposition led the United States to abandon its plan to annex the islands.
Although many Native Hawaiians signed a petition opposing annexation, Silva found that the political associations that organized it later came to support annexation.
Although Native Hawaiians’ response to annexation was long portrayed as passive, a document that Silva found reveals that many of them took part in organized resistance to it.
Although a petition that Silva located shows that many Native Hawaiians opposed annexation, it had little effect on how the US Senate treated the annexation treaty.
items.explanation: The text opens with the long-standing view that Native Hawaiians accepted annexation with little resistance and then describes the petition Silva found: more than 21,000 signatures against annexation, gathered by Native Hawaiian political associations and presented to the Senate. Choice C states both the earlier view and the evidence that revises it.

A.why_wrong: The first half is right and the petition did help defeat one treaty, but the islands were annexed through other means the following year, so the United States did not abandon annexation.

B.why_wrong: The text says the associations organized the petition against annexation; it says nothing about their later views.

D.why_wrong: The first half is right, but the text says the petition, presented to the Senate, contributed to the defeat of an annexation treaty.

sources.what: Duke University Press, Noenoe K. Silva, Aloha Betrayed (2004): Native Hawaiians organized a massive petition drive against annexation in 1897, causing the treaty to fail in the Senate; Silva rediscovered the petition while researching the book; she refutes the long-held idea that Native Hawaiians passively accepted the loss of their nation

items.notes: History. Signature count (about 21,000, Hui Aloha ʻĀina) from the UH Manoa Kue Petitions guide; the passage avoids the 95 percent figure and says the petition helped defeat the treaty, with annexation following by other means (1898 joint resolution), so no option can claim it stopped annexation.

fixes: hardened: all four options in one Although frame; A and D keep a true first clause and fail on the treaty outcome; B invents a later change of view; key paraphrased

band7.why: Planned band 6. Shared Although frame with two CON-half distractors is a band-7 trait, but the correction is signalled by a plain however, not a stance word, so band 6.

items.passage:
The following text is Charlotte Mew’s circa 1920 poem “Sea Love.” In the poem, “I mind” means “I remember,” and “glim” means a faint gleam of light.

Tide be runnin’ the great world over:
T’was only last June month I mind that we
Was thinkin’ the toss and the call in the breast of the lover
So everlastin’ as the sea.

Heer’s the same little fishes that sputter and swim,
Wi’ the moon’s old glim on the grey, wet sand;
An’ him no more to me nor me to him
Than the wind goin’ over my hand.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: The speaker mourns a lover who was lost at sea the previous June but finds some comfort in the unchanging sights and sounds of the shore.
The speaker recalls once believing that the lovers’ feelings would last as long as the sea and hopes those feelings will return as surely as the tide does.
The speaker observes that the shore has changed greatly since the previous June, much as the feelings between the speaker and the lover have.
The speaker reflects that a love once believed to be permanent has given way to indifference, though the familiar sights of the shore remain unchanged.
items.explanation: Only last June, the speaker and the lover thought their feelings were “so everlastin’ as the sea.” Now the shore looks the same, with the “same little fishes” and the moon’s “old glim,” but the two mean no more to each other than “the wind goin’ over my hand.” Choice D states this contrast between an unchanged shore and a love that has turned to indifference.

A.why_wrong: Nothing in the poem says the lover died; “him no more to me nor me to him” describes two people who have stopped caring for each other, and the speaker takes no comfort from the shore.

B.why_wrong: The speaker did once think the love would last like the sea, but the closing lines show that the two now mean nothing to each other, and the poem expresses no hope that the feeling will return.

C.why_wrong: The feelings have changed, but the shore has not: the speaker sees “the same little fishes” and the moon’s “old glim” on the sand.

sources.what: Project Gutenberg text of Charlotte Mew, The Farmer's Bride (Poetry Bookshop, 1921 edition with eleven new poems), poem Sea Love; copied exactly. Sea Love was among the new poems and first appeared in Harold Monro's Monthly Chapbook (1919 or 1920), hence circa 1920

items.notes: Poem, extended comparison (love as lasting as the sea, then as slight as the wind). Text copied exactly from the 1921 edition, including the dialect spellings and "T’was". Gloss line added as in 3.17.

fixes: hardened: key paraphrased (given way to indifference); B and C now partly right (B: the love was thought lasting, then an unsupported hope; C: the feelings changed, but the shore did not)

band7.why: Planned band 6. One extended contrast (lasting sea, passing love) carried into a general claim; distractors LIT, half-true plus unsupported hope, CON-half. Dialect is the main load, so band 6.

items.passage: In 1827, a group of Quakers in Philadelphia founded the Free Produce Society, part of a broader effort by abolitionists to boycott cotton, sugar, and other goods produced by enslaved people. Supporters of this free produce movement opened stores that sold only goods made with free labor, hoping to undermine slavery economically. Yet the movement achieved little success. Free-labor goods were generally more expensive than other goods and were sometimes difficult to obtain, and one shopkeeper often received sugar and rice of noticeably poor quality.
items.stem: According to the text, what was one difficulty faced by supporters of the free produce movement?
options: Quakers in Philadelphia were unwilling to shop in stores that sold only goods made with free labor.
Goods made with free labor usually cost more than goods produced by enslaved people did.
Stores that sold goods made with free labor could not obtain cotton, so they sold only sugar and rice.
Supporters disagreed about whether the movement should avoid sugar as well as cotton.
items.explanation: The text says that free-labor goods were usually more expensive than other goods, sometimes hard to find, and occasionally of poor quality. Choice B restates the first of these difficulties.

A.why_wrong: Philadelphia Quakers founded the Free Produce Society; the text gives no sign that they refused to shop at free-labor stores.

C.why_wrong: The text says free-labor goods were sometimes hard to find and that some sugar and rice was poor, not that stores could sell nothing but sugar and rice.

D.why_wrong: The text names cotton and sugar together among the goods the movement avoided and mentions no disagreement among supporters.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Free-produce movement: Free Produce Society founded in Philadelphia in 1827 by Thomas M'Clintock and other radical Quakers; non-slave produce was more expensive and sometimes hard to locate; storeowners received sugar with a disagreeable taste and odor and rice that was very poor

items.notes: History (abolition). One-sentence evidence in the last sentence; distractor C recombines its nouns.

fixes: source says one storeowner not infrequently received poor sugar and rice; passage changed from shopkeepers occasionally to one shopkeeper often

items.passage: Ladi Kwali was raised in Kwali, a village in northern Nigeria where pottery was traditionally practiced by women, and as a child she learned from her aunt to construct large water vessels by coiling clay by hand. In 1954 she became the first female potter at the Pottery Training Centre in Abuja (now Suleja), established two years earlier by British potter Michael Cardew. There she learned wheel throwing, glazing, and high-temperature kiln firing, yet she continued to hand-build many of her vessels.
items.stem: According to the text, what did Kwali learn at the Pottery Training Centre?
options: She learned to shape pots on a wheel and to glaze and fire them at high temperatures.
She learned to build large water pots by hand from coils of clay.
She learned to decorate her pots with designs that were unknown in her village.
She learned to give up building pots by hand and to rely entirely on the methods that Cardew introduced.
items.explanation: The text says that at the Pottery Training Centre Kwali learned to throw pots on a wheel, to glaze them, and to fire them in a kiln at high temperatures. Choice A restates this.

B.why_wrong: Kwali learned to build water pots from coils of clay as a child, from her aunt, before she joined the centre.

C.why_wrong: The text says nothing about the designs Kwali learned at the centre or about designs used in her village.

D.why_wrong: Kwali continued to build many of her vessels by hand after learning the new methods.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Ladi Kwali: born in Kwali, Gwari region of northern Nigeria, where pottery was women's work; learned coiling from her aunt; Cardew founded the Pottery Training Centre in Suleja (then Abuja) in 1952; she joined in 1954 as its first female potter and learned wheel throwing, glazing and kiln firing; her hand-built pots were glazed and fired in a high-temperature kiln

items.notes: Arts (ceramics). Distractor B is the true earlier detail the stem rules out ("at the Pottery Training Centre").

items.passage: Extensive pumping from aquifers beneath California’s San Joaquin Valley has caused the valley floor to subside in places. In 2014, geologist Colin Amos and colleagues reported a less conspicuous consequence. Using GPS measurements, they detected a broad zone of uplift, as much as 1 to 3 millimeters annually, in the rock surrounding the southern part of the valley, including the southern Sierra Nevada. Removing such an enormous volume of groundwater, the researchers explained, has reduced the load on Earth’s crust, which has flexed upward in response.
items.stem: According to the text, why is the rock around the southern San Joaquin Valley rising?
options: The sinking of the valley floor has pushed the surrounding rock upward.
Water pumped from the valley has been stored in reservoirs in the Sierra Nevada.
Earthquakes along faults near the valley have lifted the surrounding rock.
Pumping out groundwater has reduced the weight pressing down on Earth’s crust.
items.explanation: The researchers explained that removing so much groundwater has lightened the load on Earth’s crust, which has flexed upward. Choice D restates this explanation.

A.why_wrong: The text mentions both the sinking valley floor and the rising rock, but it attributes the rise to the lighter load on the crust, not to the sinking floor.

B.why_wrong: The text never says where the pumped water goes or mentions reservoirs.

C.why_wrong: The text does not mention earthquakes or faults as a cause of the uplift.

sources.what: Amos et al., Nature 509:483-486 (2014), Uplift and seismicity driven by groundwater depletion in central California: GPS shows rock uplift of up to 1-3 mm per year around the southern San Joaquin Valley, matching flexure from water-storage loss; uplift of the southern Sierra Nevada partly a consequence of groundwater depletion

items.notes: Earth science. The paper says the Sierra uplift is partly due to groundwater loss; the passage claims no more than the explanation for the zone around the valley.

items.passage: Around 850 BCE, a fire engulfed Must Farm, a cluster of wooden roundhouses built on stilts above a sluggish river in what is now eastern England. As the structures burned, their floors collapsed, and their contents fell into the muddy riverbed, where charring and waterlogging preserved them. Analyzing thousands of these artifacts, archaeologists have reconstructed the settlement’s domestic life in remarkable detail, from its interiors to its meals and fine linen clothing. The settlement, they determined, was less than a year old when it burned.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Researchers have found that Must Farm’s residents left the settlement after less than a year because the river beneath it began to flood.
Must Farm was the largest Bronze Age settlement in England, and its houses were unusually comfortable for their time.
The way Must Farm was destroyed preserved its contents so well that researchers have learned a great deal about its residents’ lives.
Archaeologists have determined that the fire at Must Farm was set by attackers from a neighboring settlement.
items.explanation: The text explains that the burning houses collapsed into the riverbed, where their contents were preserved, and that by studying these objects archaeologists have reconstructed daily life at Must Farm in remarkable detail. Choice C joins the cause of the preservation with what it has allowed researchers to learn.

A.why_wrong: The settlement was less than a year old when a fire destroyed it; the text says nothing about residents leaving because of floods.

B.why_wrong: The text describes a small cluster of houses and never ranks Must Farm’s size or comfort against other settlements.

D.why_wrong: The text does not say what caused the fire.

sources.what: University of Cambridge via ScienceDaily (March 2024): Must Farm, c. 850 BC, roundhouses on stilts above a slow-moving river; less than a year old when destroyed by fire, buildings and contents collapsing into the river; charring and waterlogging led to exceptional preservation; reports reveal domestic layouts, meals and fine flax linen

items.notes: Archaeology. Main idea spread across the destruction sentence and the research sentence. Cause of the fire is unknown in the source, so D is unsupported.

items.passage: In rural Bangladesh, the months before the rice harvest are a lean season, when farm work is scarce and many households go hungry. Economists Gharad Bryan, Shyamal Chowdhury, and Ahmed Mushfiq Mobarak offered randomly selected households $8.50 if a member migrated temporarily for work during this period. The incentive induced 22 percent of these households to send a migrant, and their consumption at home rose significantly; they were also more likely than other households to send migrants again in later years, after the incentive had ended.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Researchers found that households that sent a migrant to a city during the lean season usually stopped farming and moved there for good.
A small payment that encouraged rural households to try seasonal migration raised their consumption at home and had effects that lasted after the payment ended.
An experiment showed that the lean season in rural Bangladesh could be shortened if households received payments before the rice harvest.
Economists found that rural households in Bangladesh consume more during the lean season than households in the country’s cities do.
items.explanation: The text describes an experiment in which a payment of $8.50 led some households to send a member to work elsewhere during the lean season. Those households consumed more at home and were more likely to send a migrant again after the payments stopped. Choice B states the experiment and both of its effects.

A.why_wrong: The migration was temporary, and households sent migrants again in later years, which implies that they stayed in their villages.

C.why_wrong: The payments encouraged migration during the lean season; the text never says they changed the length of the season.

D.why_wrong: The text compares households that received the offer with other rural households, not rural households with households in cities.

sources.what: NBER w20172 / Econometrica 82:5 (2014), Bryan, Chowdhury and Mobarak: an $8.50 incentive to out-migrate during the lean season induced 22 percent of households to send a seasonal migrant; consumption at the origin rose significantly; treated households were 8-10 percentage points more likely to re-migrate 1 and 3 years later

items.notes: Social science (development economics). "spending on food and other needs" glosses consumption. Year of the experiment (2008) left out.

items.passage: Trained at the government art school in Calcutta (now Kolkata), Bengali painter Jamini Roy (1887–1972) initially worked in the European academic manner he had been taught, producing portraits and landscapes in oils. During the 1920s, however, he turned to the folk traditions of rural Bengal, particularly the bold, sweeping brushwork of Kalighat painting. Employing pigments derived from earth, minerals, and lampblack, he depicted village life and familiar religious narratives, aspiring to create art that would be accessible to ordinary people.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Roy turned from the academic style he had been taught to one rooted in Bengali folk art, hoping to reach ordinary viewers.
Roy became known for oil portraits of rural Bengalis painted in the European manner he had learned in Calcutta.
Roy taught the makers of Kalighat paintings to use colors made from earth and minerals instead of oil paints.
Roy’s paintings of village life were more popular among ordinary people than the Kalighat paintings were.
items.explanation: The text explains that Roy first painted in the academic European manner he was taught but then turned to Bengali folk art, using local materials and familiar subjects so that his art would be accessible to ordinary people. Choice A generalizes this change and its aim.

B.why_wrong: Roy painted portraits in oils early in his career, but the text says he then turned away from that manner to folk art.

C.why_wrong: Roy drew on Kalighat painting; the text does not say he taught its makers anything.

D.why_wrong: The text never compares the popularity of Roy’s paintings with that of Kalighat paintings.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Jamini Roy: taught the academic tradition at the Government College of Art, Kolkata (oils); turned to folk art, most influenced by Kalighat Pat with bold sweeping brush-strokes; experiments from 1921; aims included making art accessible to a wider section of people; used lamp black, earth and mineral pigments

items.notes: Arts (painting). Profile: training, turn, method, aim; key generalizes.

items.passage:
The following text is from Vladimir Korolenko’s 1886 novel The Blind Musician (translated by Aline Delano in 1890). Peter, a boy blind from birth, has been listening to his mother describe shapes and colors.

Evidently his brain was at work struggling with difficult problems; his unpractised imagination strove to shape from the descriptions given him a new image,—a feat which it was unable to perform. At such times Uncle Maxim always frowned with displeasure; and when the tears appeared in the mother’s eyes, and the child’s face grew pale from the effect of his intense effort, Maxim would interfere, and taking his sister’s place would tell his nephew stories, in the invention of which he would try to use only such ideas as related to sound and space. Then the face of the blind boy would grow calmer.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Peter grows tired of Maxim’s stories because they lack the vivid detail that he enjoys in his mother’s descriptions of the world.
Peter quickly learns to picture shapes and colors once Maxim explains them in terms of sound.
Peter struggles to imagine what his mother describes, and Maxim eases his distress with stories built on things Peter can perceive.
Peter’s mother becomes upset because Peter refuses to listen to her descriptions of the world.
items.explanation: The excerpt says that Peter’s imagination strove but was unable to form images from his mother’s descriptions, and that when the effort upset both mother and son, Maxim told him stories using only ideas of sound and space, which calmed him. Choice C states this situation.

A.why_wrong: Maxim’s stories calm Peter; nothing suggests that Peter tires of them.

B.why_wrong: Forming such images is described as a feat Peter’s imagination is unable to perform, and Maxim avoids shapes and colors altogether.

D.why_wrong: The mother’s tears come from watching Peter’s painful effort, not from any refusal to listen.

sources.what: Project Gutenberg text of Korolenko, The Blind Musician, translated by Aline Delano (Little, Brown, copyright 1890), part I, section IX; copied exactly, trimmed at sentence boundaries

items.notes: Literary prose (translation, 1886 Russian original). Excerpt starts mid-paragraph at a sentence boundary; context line supplies the mother's descriptions from the sentences before. Original punctuation kept, including the comma before the em dash.

items.passage: The toco toucan’s bill, enormous in proportion to the bird’s body, is permeated by blood vessels lying just beneath its surface. Using infrared thermography, biologists Glenn Tattersall, Denis Andrade, and Augusto Abe monitored bill temperatures as the air in a laboratory enclosure was gradually warmed and cooled. As conditions warmed, the toucans increased blood flow to the bill, whose surface temperature rose rapidly; as conditions cooled, they restricted the flow, and the bill cooled while the body remained warm.
items.stem: Based on the text, what is one function that the toco toucan’s bill most likely serves?
options: It allows the bird to sense small changes in air temperature before its body is affected.
It stores extra blood that the bird’s body can draw on when the air grows cool.
It stays cooler than the surrounding air, which keeps the bird’s body cool in warm weather.
It helps the bird get rid of excess body heat when the air around it is warm.
items.explanation: In warm air the toucans sent more blood to the bill, whose surface quickly heated up, and in cool air they cut the flow so the body stayed warm. A large surface that takes up warm blood when the bird is at risk of overheating most likely serves to release excess body heat.

A.why_wrong: The text describes the bill’s temperature changing in response to the air, not the bill detecting changes for the bird.

B.why_wrong: In cool air the birds reduced the blood flow to the bill; the text says nothing about the bill storing blood for the body.

C.why_wrong: In warm air the bill’s surface quickly heated up rather than staying cooler than the air.

sources.what: Revista Pesquisa FAPESP on Tattersall, Andrade and Abe, Science 2009: infrared images showed that in cold air the toucan cut the flow of heat to the beak, which cooled to retain body warmth, and in heat it increased blood flow to the beak, which dispersed excess heat

items.notes: Natural science (physiology). Premises: blood to bill in warm air, bill surface heats; flow cut in cool air to keep body warm. Unstated conclusion: the bill sheds heat. The 2023 follow-up's point that the bill can also gain heat in strong sun is not in play (no option about sunlight).

items.passage:
The following text is Edward Thomas’s 1917 poem “Tall Nettles.”

Tall nettles cover up, as they have done
These many springs, the rusty harrow, the plough
Long worn out, and the roller made of stone:
Only the elm butt tops the nettles now.

This corner of the farmyard I like most:
As well as any bloom upon a flower
I like the dust on the nettles, never lost
Except to prove the sweetness of a shower.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: The speaker regrets that the farm’s old tools have been left to rust and wishes the nettles would be cleared away.
The speaker is fond of a neglected corner of a farmyard and finds beauty even in the dust on its weeds.
The speaker prefers the flowers that bloom each spring to the nettles that grow in the farmyard.
The speaker waits eagerly for a rain shower that will wash the dust from the farmyard’s flowers.
items.explanation: The first stanza shows a farmyard corner where nettles have covered worn-out tools for many springs. In the second, the speaker says this is the corner of the farmyard he likes most and that he likes the dust on the nettles as well as any bloom on a flower. Choice B states this fondness.

A.why_wrong: The speaker likes this corner most and expresses no regret about the tools or wish to clear the nettles.

C.why_wrong: The speaker likes the dust on the nettles “as well as any bloom upon a flower.”

D.why_wrong: The dust lies on the nettles, not on flowers, and the speaker mentions a shower only as the one thing that removes the dust.

sources.what: Project Gutenberg text of Edward Thomas, Poems (Holt, 1917), poem Tall Nettles; copied exactly (first word set in capitals in the source, given here in sentence case)

items.notes: Poem, medium: a clear attitude with one figure (dust compared with a bloom). No gloss line, to stay at 2.13's length; harrow and roller read as farm tools from the list.

items.passage: The Inca Empire stretched along the Andes Mountains of South America in the 1400s and early 1500s. It stockpiled large quantities of food in storehouses called qullqas, which stood in long rows on hills near the empire’s regional centers. Builders generally positioned qullqas on dry hillsides to take advantage of drainage and wind. Each storehouse also had a ventilation system: a channel beneath the floor let air in, and an opening under the roof let it out.
items.stem: According to the text, why did Inca builders generally place qullqas on dry hillsides?
options: They wanted to take advantage of the drainage and wind there.
They wanted travelers on nearby roads to be able to see the storehouses.
They needed the flat land near regional centers for growing potatoes.
Hillsides were the only places where channels could be dug under the floors.
items.explanation: The text says that builders generally placed qullqas on dry hillsides to take advantage of drainage and wind. Choice A restates this reason.

B.why_wrong: The text never mentions roads or travelers.

C.why_wrong: The text says nothing about where crops were grown or about a shortage of flat land.

D.why_wrong: The text describes channels under the floors as part of each storehouse’s ventilation system, not as the reason for choosing hillsides.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Qullqa: qullqas generally built in connected groups on dry hillsides to take advantage of drainage and winds; ventilation by a channel beneath the floor and an opening under the roof; at Wanuku (Huanuco) Pampa 50 to 80 percent stored dried potatoes and other root crops; provincial centers had large numbers built row after row on nearby hills

items.notes: History and archaeology. Easy explicit detail; key echoes the target sentence, as easy keys do.

items.passage: Researchers had generally assumed that bioluminescent fungi glow continuously, perhaps simply as a byproduct of their metabolism. But when chemist Cassius Stevani and biologist Jay Dunlap studied Neonothopanus gardneri, a glowing mushroom from Brazil, they discovered that its light is controlled by an internal clock. To learn what the glow does, the researchers placed sticky artificial mushrooms in the forest, lighting some of them from inside with green lights. The lit artificial mushrooms trapped many more insects than the unlit ones did.
items.stem: According to the text, what happened when the researchers placed the artificial mushrooms in the forest?
options: Insects avoided the artificial mushrooms and gathered on real ones instead.
The artificial mushrooms that were unlit trapped the most insects.
The artificial mushrooms that were lit trapped many more insects than the unlit ones did.
Real mushrooms near the artificial ones stopped glowing at night.
items.explanation: The text says that the artificial mushrooms lit with green lights trapped many more insects than the unlit ones did. Choice C restates this result.

A.why_wrong: The text reports insects trapped on the artificial mushrooms and says nothing about insects gathering on real ones.

B.why_wrong: The lit artificial mushrooms, not the unlit ones, trapped many more insects.

D.why_wrong: The text says nothing about real mushrooms changing their glow near the artificial ones.

sources.what: Dartmouth Geisel School of Medicine release on Oliveira et al., Current Biology 2015: researchers had believed fungi produce light around the clock as a byproduct; N. gardneri's glow is under circadian control; lit sticky resin fake mushrooms caught many more insects than dark ones

items.notes: Natural science (mycology). Spore-dispersal interpretation left out so that the passage claims only the measured result.

items.passage:
The following text is from Ethel Turner’s 1894 novel Seven Little Australians. The seven Woolcot children make so much noise that their father, Captain Woolcot, has them eat their meals in a separate room.

It was a nursery without a nurse, too, so that partly accounted for it. Meg, the eldest, was only sixteen, and could not be expected to be much of a disciplinarian, and the slatternly but good-natured girl, who was supposed to combine the duties of nursery-maid and housemaid, had so much to do in her second capacity that the first suffered considerably.
items.stem: According to the text, what is one reason the Woolcot children are so noisy?
options: Their father encourages them to be lively at meals.
The servant who is supposed to look after them is kept busy with housework.
Meg, the eldest, is too strict with the younger children.
The nursery is too small for seven children to share.
items.explanation: The text says the household has no nurse and that the girl who is supposed to be both nursery-maid and housemaid has so much housework that her care of the children suffers. Choice B restates this reason.

A.why_wrong: Captain Woolcot has the children eat in a separate room because of their noise; nothing suggests he encourages it.

C.why_wrong: Meg is too young to be “much of a disciplinarian,” the opposite of too strict.

D.why_wrong: The text says nothing about the size of the nursery.

sources.what: Project Gutenberg text of Ethel Turner, Seven Little Australians (1894), chapter 1; copied exactly (double spaces after periods reduced to one)

items.notes: Literary prose, explicit detail with a "one reason" stem (like 1.2 and 1.9). Second paragraph of the chapter passage; the context line gives what the first paragraph says (separate meals because of the noise), which "it" refers to.

items.passage: Biologists Nichola Raihani and Amanda Ridley studied southern pied babblers, birds of southern Africa. They observed that adults often purr softly while delivering food to nestlings, but only when chicks are present. When the researchers played recorded purrs at mealtimes near certain nests, those chicks soon learned to beg upon hearing a purr. Adults that purred often also tended to lose weight. In the researchers’ view, the adults were teaching their young, at some cost to themselves.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Researchers found that pied babbler chicks learn to purr by copying the calls that adults make at mealtimes.
Researchers found that pied babblers lose weight while raising chicks because they give most of their food to the young.
Recordings of adult pied babblers can be used to raise chicks that have been separated from their parents.
Research suggests that adult pied babblers teach their chicks that a particular call signals food, even though doing so seems to cost the adults.
items.explanation: The text describes a purring call that adults make only around chicks, an experiment showing that chicks learn to link the purr with food, and the cost to adults who purr often. It ends with the researchers’ conclusion that the adults are teaching the chicks what the purr means. Choice D states this conclusion and the cost.

A.why_wrong: The chicks learn to beg when they hear a purr; the text never says they learn to purr.

B.why_wrong: The text links weight loss to purring often, not to giving away food.

C.why_wrong: The researchers played purrs near nests where adults were feeding chicks; the text says nothing about raising chicks without their parents.

sources.what: Science News (January 2008) on Raihani and Ridley, Animal Behaviour 2008: adults purr only when chicks are present; babblers that purred a lot were most likely to lose weight; chicks hearing extra purrs at mealtimes begged at the sound sooner, wrong-time chicks had little response; the researchers conclude the young are being taught

items.notes: Natural science (animal behavior). Governing claim in the last sentence, as in easy study reports.

items.passage: People often act more generously when others are watching, partly to protect their reputations. Psychologist Jan Engelmann and colleagues asked whether this tendency appears early in life and whether chimpanzees share it. Five-year-old children were given chances to share or steal stickers, and chimpanzees chances to help another chimpanzee get food or to take it away. The children shared more and stole less when a peer was watching; the chimpanzees behaved the same whether watched or not.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: An experiment found that young children, unlike chimpanzees, acted differently when others could see them.
An experiment showed that chimpanzees share more food with others when other chimpanzees are watching.
Researchers found that children share more with peers they know well than with children they have never met.
An experiment showed that children learn to share by watching how their peers behave.
items.explanation: The text describes an experiment in which five-year-old children gave more and took less when a peer was watching, while chimpanzees acted the same whether watched or not. Choice A states this finding.

B.why_wrong: The chimpanzees acted the same whether or not they were watched.

C.why_wrong: The text never compares how children treat familiar and unfamiliar peers.

D.why_wrong: The peers in the experiment watched the children; the text does not say the children learned by watching the peers.

sources.what: Engelmann, Herrmann and Tomasello, PLOS ONE 7(10): e48433 (2012): 5-year-olds share more and steal less when watched by a peer than when alone (sticker tasks); chimpanzees behave the same whether watched by a groupmate or not (food tasks)

items.notes: Social science (developmental and comparative psychology). Authors' broader claim (unique to humans among primates) left out.

items.passage: Tania León was born in Havana, Cuba, in 1943 and relocated to New York City in 1967 to continue her musical education. In 1969 she became the first music director of the Dance Theatre of Harlem, establishing the company’s music department, school, and orchestra. In 1977 she founded a community concert series for the Brooklyn Philharmonic. She has also composed numerous works, and one of them, the orchestral composition Stride, received the 2021 Pulitzer Prize for Music.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: León is known mainly for the music she wrote for performances by the Dance Theatre of Harlem.
León moved to New York City because she had been offered a job at the Dance Theatre of Harlem.
León has contributed to music both as a composer and as a founder of musical programs.
León’s piece Stride was the first work by a Cuban-born composer to be performed by an orchestra in New York City.
items.explanation: The text describes León building the Dance Theatre of Harlem’s music department, school, and orchestra, starting a concert series, and writing many works, including the Pulitzer Prize-winning Stride. Choice C sums up these two kinds of contribution.

A.why_wrong: The text says León directed the company’s music and set up its programs, not that she is known mainly for music she wrote for it.

B.why_wrong: She moved to New York City to continue her music studies and joined the company two years later.

D.why_wrong: The text says Stride won a Pulitzer Prize, not that it was the first work by a Cuban-born composer to be performed in New York.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Tania León: born in Havana in 1943; left Cuba for New York City in 1967 to continue her studies; in 1969 founding member and first music director of Dance Theatre of Harlem, establishing its music department, music school and orchestra; instituted the Brooklyn Philharmonic Community Concert Series in 1977; Stride won the 2021 Pulitzer Prize for Music

items.notes: Arts (music). Profile; key generalizes the two roles.

items.passage:
The following text is from Hector Malot’s 1878 novel Nobody’s Boy (translated by Florence Crewe-Jones in 1916).

I was a foundling. But until I was eight years of age I thought I had a mother like other children, for when I cried a woman held me tightly in her arms and rocked me gently until my tears stopped falling. I never got into bed without her coming to kiss me, and when the December winds blew the icy snow against the window panes, she would take my feet between her hands and warm them, while she sang to me.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: The narrator remembers how frightened he was of winter storms when he was a young child.
The narrator explains that a woman’s loving care led him to believe for years that she was his mother.
The narrator regrets that the woman who raised him was often too busy to comfort him.
The narrator describes how he discovered at the age of eight that the woman who raised him was not his mother.
items.explanation: The narrator says he was a foundling but thought until he was eight that he had a mother like other children, and he explains why: the woman who raised him comforted him, kissed him at bedtime, and warmed his feet while singing to him. Choice B states this main idea.

A.why_wrong: The narrator mentions December winds only to show how the woman warmed his feet; he never says he was frightened.

C.why_wrong: The woman held and rocked him whenever he cried and came to kiss him every night.

D.why_wrong: The narrator says he believed she was his mother until he was eight, but the excerpt describes her care, not how he found out the truth.

sources.what: Project Gutenberg text of Hector Malot, Nobody's Boy (Sans Famille, 1878), translated by Florence Crewe-Jones (Cupples and Leon, 1916), chapter 1; copied exactly, trimmed at a sentence boundary

items.notes: Literary prose (translation). Opening paragraph, trimmed after "sang to me"; "foundling" is left unglossed because the next sentence explains it.
